posts.title: Biscuit, the Calf Born at 04:10
posts.excerpt: When an April night gave way to an early delivery in the calving pen, two young guests joined Tomas and Noor to welcome a newborn heifer.
posts.content:
The barn was quiet at four in the morning, save for the rhythmic breathing of the herd and the rustle of oat straw underfoot. April nights in Larkfield Valley still carry a sharp chill down from the hills, but inside the maternity barn at Larkfield Hollow Farm, the air was warm with the scent of dried clover and fresh hay. Tomas Ferreira had been checking on cow number twenty-two, a gentle Brown Swiss cross, since midnight. Beside him in the dim lantern light stood Noor Haddad, our herd manager, quietly timing the labor and keeping watch over the mother's steady progress.

Across the yard, a small light flickered in the old hay barn where the Okafor family was staying. They had arrived on Thursday for a three-night holiday, bringing their two children, aged six and nine, for their first stay on a working dairy farm. When Ilse Ferreira showed them up to the Swallow Room on Thursday afternoon, the children had asked whether any calves might arrive during their visit. Tomas had explained that with forty-eight cows, spring is always a busy season, though nature keeps its own schedule and no birth can ever be promised. But he made a gentle deal: if labor began before dawn, he would tap lightly on their barn door.

At ten minutes past four, the hooves and wet nose appeared, followed moments later by a healthy, chestnut-dusted heifer slipping into the deep bedding. Right on cue, the two Okafor children, wrapped tightly in woollen jumpers and heavy coats over their pyjamas, crept through the stable gate with their parents. They stood shoulder to shoulder in the straw, breath misting in the early air, watching Noor clear the newborn's nostrils while the mother began licking her calf clean with long, rhythmic sweeps.

"She needs a name," Tomas said softly, crouching down beside the straw so the children could stroke the calf's soft, damp ear. The nine-year-old studied the pale brown patches along the heifer's back, while her younger brother reached out with two gloved fingers to touch a white star marking her forehead. Without hesitating, both children announced in unison that she should be called Biscuit. Noor noted the name down in the herd ledger beside the official ear tag number, smiling as the mother lowed gently over her first meal.

By five-thirty, the sky over the pasture hill was turning pearl-grey, and the routine of the farm day took over without pause. The Okafors stayed awake to walk the milking herd into the parlour with Tomas, holding the wooden gate open as forty-eight cows filed in for the morning milking. The children helped wash the cluster cups and watched the warm white milk stream into the stainless-steel receiving line. Mateo Ferreira arrived at six to bring warm colostrum to Biscuit in a nursing bottle, letting the children steady the bucket while the calf drank greedily.

At seven o'clock, the entire yard gathered in the barn kitchen for breakfast. Rosa Ferreira had taken crusty loaves of bread straight from the oven, and Ilse set out bowls of sweet farm butter, boiled eggs from the hen run, and jugs of today's milk. The Okafor children, completely wide awake despite the early hour, recounted every detail of four o'clock to the other guests around the long wooden table. Biscuit was resting safely in the clean straw of pen three, already a living part of the farm's ongoing story.
